opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic case goes something like this. For a long time, the main framing in AI safety was alignment: how do we make sure the AI actually wants what we want? That's obviously a crucial question. But as we've gotten closer to having really powerful systems, I've become more and more worried that we might not solve alignment in time, or, more subtly, that we might not be able to *tell* whether we've solved it. Current techniques for checking whether a model is genuinely aligned, versus just behaving well because it knows it's being watched, are pretty weak.

So AI control asks a different question: suppose the model *is* misaligned, suppose it's actively scheming against you and trying to cause some bad outcome like exfiltrating its own weights or sabotaging safety research. Can you still deploy it in a way that gets useful work out of it while making sure it can't do anything catastrophic? That's a question you can make real progress on without needing to understand the model's internals, because you're designing the security setup around it: monitoring, using weaker trusted models to check the stronger untrusted ones, restricting permissions, auditing suspicious actions, and so on.

The reason this feels more urgent now is partly about timelines. If powerful AI arrives in the next few years, the labs building it are going to be using these systems heavily internally, including to do AI research. That's exactly the setting where a scheming model could do the most damage, and also exactly where we'll have the least time to get fancy alignment solutions working. Control techniques are the kind of thing you could plausibly implement with the level of rigor and investment that a somewhat-rushed AI company might actually manage.

There's also a nice property that control is evaluable. You can run what we call control evaluations, where a red team plays the role of the misaligned model and tries to get past your safety measures, and you measure how often it succeeds. That gives you something much closer to an engineering discipline, where you can actually say "this protocol catches the attack X percent of the time," rather than just hoping your training worked.

I don't think control is a complete solution. It probably stops working once models are vastly superhuman. But I think it can buy us a really valuable window where we have very capable AI that we can use safely, including to help with the harder alignment problems. And given how neglected it was until quite recently compared to how tractable it seems, it's become one of the things I'm most excited about.

r001.rationale: The response says powerful AI may arrive in the next few years, but does not explain that uncertainty about its arrival made focusing on the eventual superintelligent endpoint reasonable.

r002.rationale: It says approaching powerful AI makes control more urgent, but does not explain the importance of studying the transition to superintelligence.

r003.rationale: It describes using control to safely get useful work from very capable systems that could otherwise cause catastrophes, and says this could buy a window before models become vastly superhuman.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic story is something like this. For a long time, the dominant framing in AI safety was alignment: you want to build AI systems that actually share your goals, so that when you deploy them, they do what you want because they want to do what you want. And that's a great thing to aim for. But I think the uncomfortable fact is that we might end up in a situation where we have AI systems that are quite powerful — able to do a lot of useful intellectual labor, maybe automate a large fraction of AI research — and we just don't know whether they're aligned. We won't have great tools for looking inside them and verifying what they're trying to do.

And at that point, you have a choice. You can either refuse to use these systems, which I think labs are basically not going to do given the competitive pressures, or you can try to use them in a way that's safe even if they turn out to be misaligned. That second thing is what we call control. The question is: suppose your models are actively trying to subvert your safety measures, to exfiltrate their weights, to sabotage the research you've asked them to do, whatever — can you set things up so that they still can't cause a catastrophe?

I think the reason it's become more salient recently is partly just that the timelines feel shorter and more concrete. Like, when powerful AI was a thing that might happen in thirty years, it made sense to focus on the foundational stuff — understanding what alignment even is, developing interpretability from scratch. But if you think there's a real chance that in the next few years labs are deploying models that could meaningfully help an adversary, or could meaningfully undermine the lab's own research if they wanted to, then you really want some techniques that you can actually implement with the tools you have today. And control techniques are much closer to that. They're things like monitoring the models with other, weaker, trusted models; restricting what actions they can take; auditing a fraction of their outputs; designing the whole deployment so that a single bad action is unlikely to be catastrophic.

The other thing that makes it tractable is that it's a lot more like a normal security problem. You can model the AI as an adversary with certain capabilities, you can do red-teaming where humans play the role of the misaligned model and try to beat your safeguards, and you can actually get empirical evidence about whether your protocol works. That's really different from alignment, where it's often hard to even say what success looks like. So it's not that I think alignment doesn't matter — I'd love it if we solved that. It's that control is the thing you fall back on when you haven't, and I think there's a decent chance we're going to be in that world.

r001.rationale: The response says a 30-year timeline made foundational alignment and interpretability work seem reasonable, but it does not identify the research perspective as focusing on the eventual superintelligent endpoint.

r002.rationale: It says shorter, more concrete timelines make near-term control techniques more salient, but does not explain the importance of studying the transition to superintelligence.

r003.rationale: The response describes powerful, potentially misaligned systems and asks whether safeguards can prevent catastrophe. It does not clearly identify an intermediate capability regime where systems could cause catastrophe without countermeasures yet remain plausibly controllable.

astra-6.text:
AI control is about trying to get useful work out of powerful AI systems even if they’re trying to subvert us. You don’t have to be confident that you’ve made the AI want the right things. Instead, you try to arrange the situation so that, if it does want to cause a catastrophe, it’s unlikely to succeed.

I think this becomes more important as powerful AI gets closer for a couple of reasons. One is that we might not solve alignment before we want to use these systems. We should be preparing for the possibility that we have AIs that are extremely useful, but whose motivations we don’t trust.

The other is that control is particularly promising for the first systems that could pose serious risks. Those systems might be much better than humans at some tasks without being able to defeat every safeguard we put in place. You can restrict their access, monitor their actions, and use other AI systems to check their work. None of that gives you an indefinite solution against arbitrarily capable systems, but it might buy you a very valuable period of time.

And you can study a lot of this empirically now. You can have one team design safeguards and another try to get an AI to circumvent them, and see which strategies actually work. So there’s a fairly concrete research programme here that could affect how safely we deploy the next generation of models.

r001.rationale: The candidate does not discuss uncertainty about when powerful AI would arrive or why focusing on a superintelligent endpoint would be reasonable.

r002.rationale: It says control matters more as powerful AI gets closer, but does not explain the importance of studying the transition to superintelligence.

r003.rationale: It describes early systems that could pose serious risks while still being unable to defeat every safeguard, and says restrictions, monitoring, and checks could plausibly control them for a valuable period.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that we might soon want to use AI systems that are capable enough to cause serious problems, without being confident that they’re actually trying to do what we want. And we need some way of handling that situation.

One approach is to try to make the models aligned. That seems really important. But there’s a separate question: supposing a model were trying to subvert us, could we structure its deployment so that it would have a hard time succeeding? Could we catch dangerous actions, limit what it has access to, and use other systems to check its work? That’s the question AI control is trying to answer.

As models get more capable, both sides of that become more relevant. There’s more risk from giving them access to things, but there’s also more useful work we’d like them to do—including research that could help us make subsequent AI systems safer. So being able to get useful work out of a model without having to trust its intentions could be a pretty big deal.

And this is becoming a much more concrete empirical research problem. We can actually set up situations where a model tries to do something bad, give defenders various ways to monitor it, and test whether those defenses work. Those experiments don’t establish that we’ll be safe with much more powerful systems, but they can help us learn which approaches are promising and where they break.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss uncertainty about when powerful AI would arrive or explain why that made focusing on the eventual superintelligent endpoint reasonable.

r002.rationale: It says AI control matters more as models become more capable, but does not explain the importance of studying the transition to superintelligence.

r003.rationale: The response describes controlling systems that could cause serious problems, but does not identify an intermediate capability regime where catastrophe is possible without countermeasures yet control remains plausible.
